paragraphs: In the spring of the first year of Yuanxing, the wild shepherd’s purse outside Jiankang had begun to bloom white. Days of unbroken rain had darkened its roots with mud, yet women still bent to dig it up. Behind them a crowd waited for the gates to open. Their bundles lay piled beneath the Vermilion Bird Gate, spilling from the rain shelters into the wagon ruts of the highway.

The soldiers changing watch on the walls looked out every quarter-hour. They feared Huan Xuan’s army advancing from the west as much as the refugees in their soaked clothing. The gate captain had received two orders the previous night: Sima Yuanxian forbade the admission of people without household registration, while the governor of Danyang ordered the gates to take in the sick and infirm. Both documents bore vermilion seals; both had arrived that morning. The captain folded the second one, tucked it beneath his scabbard, and obeyed only the first.

An old woman knelt outside the gate, her knees blue with cold, holding up a torn certificate identifying her as an army dependent. Her son had joined the Northern Garrison years ago. He had guarded grain at Jingkou, then patrolled the Huai with his unit; for three years she had heard nothing from him. A girl beside her held an edge of her straw rain cape. Suddenly the girl picked a scrap of paper from the gutter. Rain had blurred the ink, leaving only eight characters legible: Ask Qin to end the turmoil. Open the granaries and save the people.

A gate soldier reached to snatch it, and the frightened girl hid it inside her clothes. As they struggled at the gateway, the captain approached and recognized the words at once. More than a dozen copies had been carried from Danyang’s residential lanes to the Censorate the previous night. By morning they had reached even beyond the walls. People inside the city printed them, refugees outside picked them up, and no one knew where the hand that first wrote them had been.
“The gate will not open,” said the captain.
The old woman raised her head with difficulty. “The official paper says you’ll take in the sick.”
“Can you read?”
“No. My son can. Before he left, he taught me to recognize the government seals.”

The captain lowered his eyes. He pushed the Danyang governor’s order half an inch deeper beneath the scabbard. When the gate bar fell, there was no battle cry outside, only the sound of many people pounding together on the doors. Through the rain-soaked timbers, it sounded like muffled drums.

That afternoon news that Huan Xuan’s vanguard was nearing Stone City reached the government offices. Sima Yuanxian stood under the corridor eaves, staring west into the sallow sky. Servants carried past a bronze brazier; the damp had long since smothered its incense cakes. Without looking at it, he demanded Liu Laozhi’s campaign map from a military clerk.

Northern Garrison banners filled the approaches to Xinting, not far from the imperial city. The more Sima Yuanxian studied the map, the angrier he became. “His men are outside the city. Why have they not moved a step in three days?”

The clerk replied that Liu Laozhi wanted grain, payment of arrears, and a written ruling: after Huan Xuan was defeated, the army command must not be prosecuted for moving troops without authorization.
“What else does he want? Shall we make him Director of the Secretariat?” Sima Yuanxian flung his wooden ruler to the ground.

Sima Daozi looked more ill than ever. Leaning against his desk, he coughed for a long while, then ordered someone to retrieve the ruler. He spoke Liu Laozhi’s name softly. He had seen the Northern Garrison in its infancy: northerners driven south, armed with armor and spears; every time Xie Xuan called out a battalion, several great Jiankang houses had to scrape together another consignment of grain. The army had since fought countless battles for the court. The state granaries still owed it months of rations, while the palace imagined that an edict alone could send it off to die.
“Give him grain,” said Sima Daozi.
“There is none in the granaries.”
“Borrow it.”
“From whom?”

Sima Daozi looked up at his son. The keenness that had once marked the young man’s brow had turned entirely to agitation. The southern magnates kept their stores locked, the grain barges were stranded on the river, and Jingzhou’s army was nearly at their gates. Another day, and no one could be sure who in this hall would still have the power to issue an edict.

In the Xinting camp, two letters lay before Liu Laozhi. Sima Yuanxian offered him the title of Great General Who Conquers the West; Huan Xuan offered command of all forces north of the Yangtze. Neither side’s envoy would deliver grain first, though both were perfectly willing to raise the offered rank by another degree.
Liu Laozhi lifted the palace letter’s clay seal with the point of his knife. “How many days of rations can Jingkou supply?” he asked his quartermaster.
“Eleven. Eight if the sick and the soldiers’ families eat with the men.”
“And the five thousand shi the court promised?”
“The seal verification has not arrived.”

Liu Laozhi set down the letters. His officers had divided into factions. Some wanted to rescue the throne, some to go over to Huan Xuan, and some to lead their own troops back to Jingkou rather than perish for either the Sima or the Huan family. In the end every man had spoken of rank, lineage, and the imperial ancestral temples. Only the quartermaster’s tally of grain had not risen or fallen by so much as half a dou.

Liu Yu sat near the entrance of the command tent. The soles of his boots still carried traces of mud from the previous year’s floods north of the Huai. The crossing permit he had brought back from the Qin camp, the relief register for seven wounded soldiers, and his countersignature authorizing Qin grain to enter Xuyi had all given the censors grounds to question him. Liu Laozhi had shielded him for a time, but later had seized his military papers more than once to interrogate him for releasing Du Qian without permission. Old favors bound the two men; a breach now lay between them that could no longer be ignored.
“Deyu,” an old general called him by name, “you have been to the north. Tell us: when Huan Xuan comes, do we submit or stand?”
“First, secure the grain at Jingkou.”
Someone sneered. “Huan Xuan wants Jiankang. What have your few grain depots to do with that?”

“If the troops retreat from Jiankang, they eat from those depots. If they enter the city, they eat from them too.” Liu Yu indicated three post roads on the campaign map. “Let the stores fall into the hands of marauding soldiers, and the court’s edict may reach us, but the army will never reach its destination.”
“You are stalling.”

Liu Yu did not argue. He took out a creased, rain-damp family letter and laid it beside the grain accounts. It came from the elderly mother of a soldier. Men had arrived at the estate to levy grain again, supposedly for the court’s war preparations. She asked her son what the family was to eat once it had paid in full. At the end she added another question: was it true that households who came north from the south could obtain registration north of the Huai?
The tent fell silent. Liu Laozhi glanced at the letter, then looked up at Liu Yu. “Do you believe in what they do across the river?”

“Some things are worth learning. In other matters they cheat people just the same. I saw Qin soldiers beat refugees, and I saw the officials responsible lose their pay and face punishment. Here, we have case files, but an inquiry often stops at the first threshold.”
Liu Laozhi asked, “Will you defeat Huan Xuan for me, then?”

“If you give the order, General, I will go. But first tell the soldiers where their grain will come from and who will compensate the wounded and the dead. Three groups of men in this army have already failed to collect their old arrears. Promise more pay that exists only on paper, and they will not believe you.”
Liu Laozhi swept aside the papers on his table and dismissed the generals. Only as Liu Yu passed him did he speak quietly. “Since when has war waited for accounts to be settled?”
“If they cannot be settled, the men who march should at least know what is owed.”

Liu Laozhi’s hand came to rest on his sword. He did not wish to kill this young subordinate. Yet he suddenly understood that one day the army Liu Yu wanted would be different from the army he himself commanded.

Visitors came to Zhu Xu’s former house in Xiangyang as well. One man had an arm wrapped in old cloth. He had once held the city wall beside Zhu Xu, and of his family of four he was now the only survivor. His voice shook when he spoke of Fu Jian. During Qin’s siege, they had cursed the Qin army more bitterly than anyone; now three different armies had come in succession to seize grain from his village, and he found himself wishing to send Chang’an a letter asking for help.

Zhu Xu had lived for years as a resident guest in Qin lands, but after returning south he had never treated his captivity and surrender as a badge of distinction. He remembered Fu Jian’s restraint toward prisoners; he remembered, too, the Jin soldiers who fell in Xiangyang’s gateway when the city was taken. “If Qin troops enter the south,” he asked, “and your village lies between the armies, who will shield you from the arrows?”
The man bent double in tears. “General, we have already shielded against everything we could.”

Zhu Xu had no answer. He rose and put on his straw cape. Beneath the window lay a copy of a grain voucher sent from Xuyi bearing Liu Yu’s countersignature. Zhu Xu remembered this clearly: when twenty thousand shi of Qin grain crossed the Huai, not one Qin unit had accompanied the boats. Jin officials had inspected the grain themselves and made their own agreement for repayment. Such dealings were still possible. Letting an army cross the Yangtze would be another matter entirely.

By the time he reached the Vermilion Bird Ferry, Huan Xuan’s horns could be heard from the west. Crowds pressed together on the bridge. Those waving Jin flags jostled against people carrying scraps reading “Ask Qin,” and blades were about to be drawn. Zhu Xu moved among them. A child was knocked down at his feet. He stooped to lift the child and found blood running from the forehead, mingling with rain as it dripped onto his sleeve.

Someone recognized him and called for him to say a just word on behalf of the south. An elderly scholar nearby denounced those who would “bring in northern barbarians to destroy the state.” Another man immediately shouted back that someone born to a great house and a rich stipend knew nothing of hunger or cold. Zhu Xu listened, then took a much-crumpled leaflet calling for troops. Instead of tearing it up before the crowd, he smoothed it out for them to see. More than a dozen fingerprints crowded the back; some of the ink was already blurred beyond recognition.
“How many families are represented here?” he asked.
No one answered. A woman at the back said there had been six. They had first written it to ask the official granaries to release grain. Only later had someone added the word “Qin.”

Zhu Xu returned the paper. The river below the bridge ran muddy, and the palace guards behind the gates still watched the crowd. “If you are asking for grain, I will go to the granary and demand it with you,” he told the woman. “If you are asking for soldiers, I have no authority to make that promise on your behalf or on behalf of this whole city.”
“And if the granary stays shut?”

Zhu Xu turned toward the closed gate. He had once pursued Lu Xiaoqi’s case under a personal edict from Sima Yao; after the emperor’s death the edict was locked away in the inner archives, and many of those implicated had still received no redress. He knew that a piece of paper could not necessarily open this gate.
“First make them see who is starving to death outside it,” he said.

A few people offered to go with him. Many more remained where they stood. Some thought him timid, some trusted him, and some wanted nothing more than somewhere they could obtain a bowl of porridge at once. Just then the crash of an opening gate rang from the western side of the city. Huan cavalry entered along the main street, their officers passing on a new order against looting. Zhu Xu handed the injured child to a healer and withdrew with several wounded people toward the bridge.

Huan Xuan rode into Jiankang without a canopy over his carriage. Along the way he saw people sheltering beneath the eaves, fresh proclamations promising public order curling in the rain, and a few leaflets asking Qin for help still hanging from the bridge rails. An attendant called them the trickery of northern spies. Huan Xuan instead ordered the sheets collected and preserved so that their handwriting and paper could be examined at his residence.
“If spies wrote them, we can find out,” said Huan Xuan. “If they were written by people of this city, there is even more reason to investigate.”

No great looting took place in the imperial precinct that night, and military officials sealed and guarded the Stone City granaries separately. Huan Xuan had kept the first prohibition he issued on entering the city. Yet the sick outside were still refused admission, and the tax granaries had not been opened. The morning watch changed. The old woman’s army-dependent certificate was examined once more, but her feet were now too swollen for her shoes.

Zhu Xu lifted her onto his back and walked toward the gateway. The gate captain barred him with a spear, saying the new administration required names to be registered at an outer reception camp. Zhu Xu asked whether that camp had a healer. The captain replied that the necessary documents were still being expedited.

He did not put the old woman down. He asked the girl to write her name on the registration board. Unable to write, the little girl stood on tiptoe, gripping the ink brush for a long time before producing two crooked marks. Zhu Xu told a clerk to record their former home and the woman’s condition, then sat beside the threshold to wait.

At Xinting, Liu Yu received news from the city. Liu Laozhi had decided, for the time being, not to come to Sima Yuanxian’s aid. The Northern Garrison’s banners still stood where they had stood before; only the man giving orders inside the city had changed. Liu Yu gathered seventeen soldiers and ordered each to take a literate army clerk back to Jingkou to audit the accounts. No one was to use the inspection of granaries as an excuse to seize civilian grain. The central command had not yet approved this order.
One man asked, “What if the general punishes you for it?”
“Send him the ledgers. Let him see how much grain we have taken, and how many lives we still owe.”

The seventeen went off carrying bundles of records. Alone, Liu Yu placed the medical record of Cao Qi, which he had brought back from Qin territory, beneath his map. Day was breaking. Smoke still lingered over the western part of the city. Not a single northern banner had crossed the Huai, yet because of those scraps of paper everyone in Jiankang was talking about the north.

On the following day Huan Xuan sent an envoy to summon Zhu Xu to discuss affairs north of the river. The messenger found him at the Vermilion Bird Gate, holding a medicine bowl steady for the old woman, who was burning with fever. More refugees had arrived outside. Not having heard that anyone had been admitted to the palace, they still stood in the rain asking: when would the city open?
